sections.html:
An Ohio seller's bill at closing has two parts: a few charges written into the Revised Code, and whatever the purchase contract hands to the seller. The statutory items are the county auditor's conveyance fee, an optional county transfer tax, a small per-parcel transfer fee and, on paper filings, any recording charge the contract puts on you. The contract side covers your mortgage payoff and prorations for taxes and similar items.

Use the table as a checklist of the charges the legislature set, then ask the title agent for the line items on your own closing statement.

Ohio charges set by statute that touch a home sale
ChargeAmount
Conveyance fee, paid to the county auditor (R.C. 319.54(G)(3))$1 or ten cents per $100 or fraction, whichever is greater
Optional county real property transfer tax (R.C. 322.02(A))Up to thirty cents per $100
Auditor's entry of a land transfer (R.C. 319.54(G)(2))Fifty cents per transfer
Recording the first two pages of an instrument (R.C. 317.32(A))$17 base plus $17 housing trust fund
Each added page (R.C. 317.32(A))$4 base plus $4 housing trust fund
Optional document preservation surcharge (R.C. 317.32(A))Up to $5 per instrument

The grantor, which means the seller. Section 319.202 puts the fee under 319.54(G)(3), plus any Chapter 322 transfer tax, on the grantor at the moment the deed is delivered. The deed makes two stops, the auditor first and the recorder second.

The fee is figured on "value." That means everything paid or promised for the property, with any mortgage or vendor's lien counted in. For a gift, value is the open-market price a willing buyer and willing seller would agree on. Willfully falsifying the stated value is prohibited.

sections.h2: Do Ohio counties charge different conveyance rates?
sections.html:
Yes. The state sets the floor. Commissioners in each county may add up to thirty cents per hundred dollars under section 322.02. To adopt it, the board must hold two public hearings and publish notice, and the resolution is generally open to a referendum.

Two counties show how the printed figure looks. Morrow County shows $4.00 per thousand for real estate and for manufactured homes alike. Muskingum County prints the same $4.00 per thousand. Its method is the sale price times 0.004, rounded to the nearest ten cents, with a $0.50 per parcel transfer fee added. Rates vary elsewhere, so check your own county auditor's real estate transfer page or phone the office before you estimate proceeds.

sections.h2: Transfers that skip the conveyance fee
sections.html:
The exemptions in section 319.54(G)(3) matter most to families and estates. They include:

  • A deed whose only purpose is to confirm or correct one already recorded.
  • A gift from one spouse to the other, or from a parent to a child or the child's spouse.
  • A transfer among heirs at law or devisees of a common decedent when no money is paid.
  • A deed to the trustee of a trust whose maker kept an unlimited power to revoke.
  • A transfer that involves no money or other valuable consideration and is not a gift.
  • A transfer by court order, unless it results from a sale made under that order.
  • An interest worth $100 or less.

For an exempt transfer, the statement of value only has to give the reason for the exemption.

The recorder's charges come from section 317.32, and the base and housing trust fund amounts are the same in every county. Pages are counted by the caption page and any partial page, measured at eight and one-half by fourteen inches, so a deed with exhibits costs more than a short one.

Fees are due when the instrument is presented, except electronic filings, which may be settled afterward by electronic funds transfer or a similar method. The statute leaves open which side of a sale pays for recording the deed. Read your purchase contract, or ask the title agent, to see who is assigned that line.

Ohio real estate taxes come in two installments, and the default due dates in section 323.12 are December 31 and June 20. Counties set their own closing dates, which can differ.

On a sale, the owner of record receives the bill, and taxes should be prorated at closing. The seller credits the buyer for the prorated share on the closing statement. Muskingum County's treasurer describes it that way, and other counties work much the same. Your title agent computes the actual figure.

Two other items can surface in the deed's statement of value. If the home received a tax reduction under section 323.152, the statement must address it. If the land was in the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program, a recoupment charge under section 5713.34 may apply when it stops qualifying.

sections.h2: Mortgage payoff and the lien release
sections.html:
Your payoff is taken from the sale proceeds and sent to the lender. Under section 5301.36, the lender must then record a release of the mortgage within ninety days of satisfaction, and the contract can let it recover the recording fee from the borrower.

If no release is recorded, the owner can send a written notice. The lender then has fifteen days before damages of $100 per day begin, capped at $5,000. A mortgagor may also recover $250 in damages for a late release. After closing, look up the county recorder's index to confirm the release posted.

Sellers of homes with as many as four dwelling units fill out the state's property disclosure form and give the buyer a signed copy, as section 5302.30 requires. The form covers water supply, sewer, structure, hazardous materials and known defects.

If the form reaches the buyer only after the contract is signed, the buyer has three business days to back out. That right ends at the earlier of thirty days after acceptance or closing. Exceptions cover court-ordered transfers, estate fiduciary transfers, and a seller who inherited the home and has not lived there in the past year. When the buyer is borrowing, federal rules require the lender to provide a Closing Disclosure three business days before closing, and its seller-side lines show credits and prorations.

sections.h2: What a seller gets back at closing
sections.html:
A closing statement runs both directions. Besides charges, a seller can be owed money, most often a refund of taxes or other items prepaid beyond the closing date. The buyer's Closing Disclosure shows costs the seller prepaid that the buyer reimburses, and prior taxes and fees the seller owes that the buyer will pay later and the seller covers now. Tax prorations land on those lines.

A seller may also agree to contribute to the buyer's closing costs, either as a general amount or as named "Seller Paid" items. If you offer a credit to win a sale, have the figure written into the contract and carried to the final statement so the two match.

Your net is the sale price less the payoff, the statutory fees above, any agreed credits and the tax proration. Ask the title agent for a draft statement several days before closing, then compare each line against the table on this page and the county's printed rate. A cash sale tends to trim the list, since there is no lender-driven paperwork on the buyer's side to wait on.

faqs.q: What is the Ohio conveyance fee?
faqs.a: Revised Code 319.54(G)(3) sets it at the greater of $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value. A county can layer up to thirty cents per hundred on top, and both land on the seller.

faqs.q: Does Ohio have a state transfer tax?
faqs.a: Ohio's charge is collected by the county auditor rather than as one flat state rate. The statutory fee has a floor, and counties may levy an optional tax capped at thirty cents per hundred dollars.

faqs.q: Who pays recording fees on an Ohio sale?
faqs.a: The statute sets the amount and leaves the assignment to the contract. Check the settlement statement or ask the title agent which side carries the deed's recording fee.

faqs.q: How fast must an Ohio lender record the mortgage release?
faqs.a: Within ninety days after the mortgage is satisfied. If it is late, the owner can give written notice, and the lender then has fifteen days to record before daily damages start.

faqs.q: Are inherited-house sales exempt from the Ohio disclosure form?
faqs.a: Sometimes. The disclosure statute exempts a seller who got the property by inheritance and has not lived in it within the past year, as well as transfers by estate fiduciaries.
